newsitem.title: TANZANIA: First non-Rwandan appears before genocide tribunal.
newsitem.headline: First non-Rwandan appears before genocide tribunal.

text.p: A Belgian appeared before a tribunal into Rwanda's genocide on Thursday, the first non-Rwandan seized on suspicion of involvement in the slaughter in 1994.

The tribunal earlier extended detention of former Rwandan prime minister Jean Kambanda for 30 days after he made no objection. It promised to rule on four other suspects including the Belgian later on Thursday.
Belgian George Ruggiu covered his face with a headdress as he entered the courtroom at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda in the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha.
Asked to introduce himself, he told the court he was born on October 12, 1957, in Belgium and was working as a journalist for Rwanda's Radio Television des Milles Collinnes (RTLM) in Kigali in 1994.

Prosecutor Jan Stewart of Canada said he wanted a 30-day extension of Ruggiu's detention because when he was arrested in Nairobi he had a South African passport but he had changed his identity and physical appearance, apparently to evade capture.

Defence lawyer Mohamed Aouini said Ruggiu wanted an address book confiscated from him to be returned and an hour of exercise per day instead of only 15 minutes. He also said his client had been interviewed by the tribunal but received no written copy.
Ruggiu and Kambanda were among eight suspects arrested in Kenya last month and handed over to the tribunal in Arusha.

Six who appeared in court on Thursday were not indicted by the tribunal and are only suspected of having participated in the genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates in Rwanda in 1994.
The six were therefore only initially detained for 30 days.
Presiding Judge Laity Kama of Senegal read out a letter from Kambanda, 42, saying he did not want a defence lawyer and was not opposed to a 30-day extension of detention as sought by the prosecution.
He extended Kambanda's detention for 30 days and appointed Josette Kadji as his defence counsel.
Prosecutors said the extra time was necessary due to the case's complexity, difficulties in investigating and the need for a precise indictment against him.

The other four appearing on Thursday were former newspaper editor Hassan Ngeze, Sylvain Nsabimana, a former government official in the southern Rwandan city of Butare, Gratien Kabiligi, a former colonel in the army's general staff, and Aloys Ntabakuze, a former commander of a commando battalion.

Stewart said Kabiligi, 45, was using a false name when he was arrested and had a Zairean passport but Rwanda's government had opened its archives so the prosecution hoped to gain more information to indict him.
He said Ntabakuze was also using a Zairean passport with a false name but the defence asked for his release so he could protect his family stranded in Nairobi without travel papers.
Kama agreed to postpone the hearing on Ngeze until next Monday after the defence said it was not ready to defend him.
The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda was set up in 1994 to bring to justice leaders of the 1994 genocide sparked by the assassination of military strongman Juvenal Habyarimana.
A total of 21 suspects are held in the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha, the tribunal's headquarters. Three trials are now underway and a total of 23 suspects have been indicted.
